counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In one of the largest foreign corruption settlements in U.S. history, engineering and defense contracting giant KBR Inc. has agreed to plead guilty and pay $579 million in total penalties for its role in a decade-long scheme to bribe Nigerian officials to secure lucrative gas contracts.

The Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced the historic plea agreement on Tuesday, capping a massive federal investigation into corporate misconduct spanning more than ten years.

KBR, a former subsidiary of Houston-based oilfield services giant Halliburton, admitted to violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) by systematically funneling more than $180 million in bribes to senior Nigerian government officials between 1994 and 2004. 

The bribes were used to secure four major contracts worth over $6 billion to build a liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant on Bonny Island, Nigeria.

### "Suitcases of Cash"

According to federal court filings, the bribery network was elaborate, secretive, and orchestrated at the highest executive levels. 

KBR participated in a four-company joint venture known as TSKJ—consisting of KBR, French firm Technip, Italian firm Snamprogetti, and Japan’s JGC Corporation. Prosecutors said TSKJ executives met regularly in cities across Europe, including London, Paris, and Amsterdam, to coordinate the bribe payments.

To hide the money trail, the joint venture hired two agents—a UK-based solicitor and a Japanese trading company—to funnel tens of millions of dollars in "consulting fees" through shell companies registered in tax havens like Gibraltar and the British Virgin Islands. 

In reality, court documents reveal, that money was used to bribe high-ranking Nigerian executive branch officials, members of the state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), and political party leaders. In some instances, bribes were delivered directly as physical cash in suitcases.

"Today’s guilty plea by KBR ends a long and disgraceful chapter in corporate history," said Acting Assistant Attorney General Rita M. Glavin of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. "This company engaged in a massive, multi-year scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials to win lucrative engineering and construction contracts. The message of today's enforcement action is clear: corporate bribery will not be tolerated."

### The Fall of a Top Executive

The central figure in the scheme, former KBR Chief Executive Officer Albert "Jack" Stanley, previously pleaded guilty in federal court to conspiracy charges for leading the bribery effort. 

Stanley, who was fired from KBR in 2004, admitted to secretly negotiating the bribe amounts directly with top Nigerian officials and pocketing millions in kickbacks himself. He currently faces up to seven years in prison and is awaiting sentencing.

Under the terms of the settlement, KBR will pay a $402 million criminal fine to the Department of Justice. Additionally, KBR and its former parent company, Halliburton, will jointly pay $177 million in disgorgement of profits to the SEC.

Halliburton, which fully spun off KBR in 2007, released a statement emphasizing that the illegal actions occurred prior to the separation and that the company had cooperated fully with government investigators. 

Current KBR Chief Executive William P. Utt said in a statement that the company is eager to put the legacy issue behind it. 

"We are pleased to reach a resolution with the government," Utt said. "The actions that led to this settlement were committed by former employees who violated our code of business conduct. Today’s KBR is a very different company, committed to the highest ethical standards."

### A Warning to Wall Street

Legal experts say the record-setting penalty signals a aggressive new era of federal enforcement against American corporations operating abroad. 

"This settlement sends a seismic shockwave through boardrooms across the country," said CNN Senior Legal Analyst Jeffrey Toobin. "The Justice Department is sending an unequivocal signal: if you bribe foreign officials to get an unfair edge in global business, the U.S. government will hunt you down, hit you with massive fines, and put your executives in prison."

As part of the plea agreement, KBR has agreed to retain an independent compliance monitor for three years to overhaul its internal controls and ensure strict adherence to anti-bribery laws moving forward.

Meanwhile, federal prosecutors hinted that the investigation remains ongoing, leaving open the possibility of further charges against individual executives and international partners involved in the Bonny Island project.

But behind the multi-billion-dollar energy complex lay one of the most extensive international bribery networks ever prosecuted by federal authorities.

Between 1995 and 2004, KBR—then operating as Kellogg Brown & Root, a subsidiary of Halliburton—entered into a joint venture with three foreign partners to secure contracts to build and expand the giant natural gas plant on the West African coast. To guarantee winning the contracts, which totaled more than $6 billion, executives orchestrated a sophisticated scheme that funneled over $180 million in bribes to high-ranking Nigerian government and military officials.

The illicit payments were routed through an intricate web of offshore shell companies, a London-based lawyer acting as a middleman, and Japanese trading firms.

The unraveling of the scheme marked a turning point in the enforcement of the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA). Federal prosecutors exposed how corporate leadership turned a blind eye—and in some cases actively directed—the flow of corrupt funds to eliminate competition in the resource-rich Niger Delta.

In 2009, KBR and Halliburton agreed to a landmark $579 million settlement with the Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission. KBR pleaded guilty to a four-count charge of conspiring to violate the FCPA. 

The legal consequences extended beyond corporate fines to personal accountability. Albert "Jack" Stanley, the former CEO of KBR who was widely viewed as the architect of the bribery ring, was sentenced to two and a half years in federal prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy charges.

While KBR has since spun off from Halliburton and overhauled its corporate compliance structures, the Nigerian natural gas cases remain a watershed moment in corporate law—a stark reminder of the devastating financial and legal risks of doing business through backchannel corruption.

*CNN's Marcus Vance contributed to this report.*
